title: Count with one switch at a time
hook: Can you count 0 to 7 flipping just one bit per step?

doesNotKnow: that a counting order exists where only one bit changes per step

misconception: Counting up in any base-2 order needs several bits to change at once at some steps.
objective: The learner can explain that Gray code (g = n XOR (n >> 1)) changes exactly one bit per step, so counting 0 to 7 takes 7 flips against binary's 11, and 3 to 4 flips one bit instead of three.

claims.text: Going from 3 to 4, binary flips all three bits (011 to 100) and Gray code flips one (010 to 110).
claims.source: Builder's node script (2026-10-14, algo2-sc) and gray() in Demo.tsx: 3 XOR 1 = 2 = 010, 4 XOR 2 = 6 = 110; popcount(011 XOR 100) = 3, popcount(010 XOR 110) = 1. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node: gray(3)=010, gray(4)=110; popcount(011^100)=3, popcount(010^110)=1. Reveal renders str(gray(3)) to str(gray(4)).

claims.text: Counting 0 to 7, binary makes 11 bit flips and Gray code makes 7, exactly one per step.
claims.source: Builder's node script: Gray sequence 000 001 011 010 110 111 101 100; binary flips per step 1 2 1 3 1 2 1 (11), Gray 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 (7). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node: Gray sequence 000 001 011 010 110 111 101 100; binary flips 1 2 1 3 1 2 1 = 11, Gray 7 x 1 = 7.

claims.text: Gray code: g = n XOR (n shifted right one place).
claims.source: Definition of the binary-reflected Gray code. One bit per step: going from n to n+1 flips a run of trailing bits (lowest 0 and the 1s below it); g(n) XOR g(n+1) = (n XOR (n+1)) XOR ((n XOR (n+1)) >> 1), and n XOR (n+1) = 2^(t+1) - 1, so the result is 2^t, a single bit. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Stage rule matches gray() = n ^ (n >> 1). Derivation re-checked; own node check: g(n) XOR g(n+1) has one bit for all n < 4096.

claims.text: If a sensor reads halfway between two marks, a Gray reading can be off by one position, never a jumble of bits.
claims.source: Adjacent positions differ in one bit, so a reading taken mid-change can only return one of the two neighbouring codes. In binary, 011 -> 100 changes three bits, and a mid-change read can mix them into any of 8 codes (e.g. 111 = 7). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Follows from c3: neighbours differ in one bit, so a read during one transition gives one of the two neighbouring codes (ideal per-bit sensing). Search snippets on encoders (control.com 'An Introduction to Gray Code for Encoders'; Omron FAQ) say the same: a misread is at most one step.

claims.text: Rotary encoders use Gray code for this reason.
claims.source: Frank Gray, 'Pulse code communication', US patent 2,632,058 (filed 1947, granted 1953): brief marks the number 'check before building'; not checked by the builder and not quoted on the stage. Absolute rotary encoders commonly use Gray code (e.g. Knuth, TAOCP vol. 4A, section 7.2.1.1, from memory). Needs a fact-checker to open a source. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Patent US 2,632,058 NOT opened (patents.google.com blocked); search snippets give 'Pulse Code Communication', F. Gray, filed 13 Nov 1947, granted 17 Mar 1953, but the patent is about pulse-code transmission, not encoders, and is not on the stage. The learner sentence (encoders use Gray code to avoid mid-transition misreads) is corroborated by search snippets from several independent sources (control.com, Omron, NIST DADS entry with a rotary-encoder figure); no page opened. Knuth TAOCP 4A not opened.

recall.question: A dial sensor might be read just as it moves from one position to the next. Why number its positions in Gray code?
options: Neighbouring positions differ in one bit, so a half-read is off by at most one
Gray code uses fewer bits than binary
Gray code numbers are larger, so errors are easier to spot
recall.why: Only one bit changes between neighbours, so a reading caught mid-change is one of the two neighbouring positions, not a random code.
